headline: ABS data shows strong June employment growth driven by part-time workers and post-Iran uncertainty rebound, but underemployment is rising
reasoning: Sean Crick from the ABS explained that the 76,000 jump in June employment was partly driven by a rebound from uncertainty in April around the Iran conflict, with part-time employment — particularly among males and younger cohorts — accounting for 47,000 of those jobs. He noted that the number of people remaining employed month-to-month and those transitioning from job-attached-but-not-working into employment were both running above seasonal norms, suggesting idiosyncratic catch-up dynamics. However, underemployment rose to 6.5% from a recent low of 5.7% in December, indicating that many of the new part-time workers want more hours than they are getting. Hours worked growth was notably softer than headline employment growth, consistent with an increase in part-time rather than full-time work. Crick acknowledged the narrative that rising participation may be demand-driven, with cost-of-living pressures pushing more Australians — particularly women and youth — into the labour market.
quote: Obviously we saw quite a strong increase in the number of number of employed people. And there's a few factors in there. As you know. You know the part time increase was 47,000. We saw an increase. Um, you know, particularly males in part time drove a lot of that increase, and we saw a big increase also from the the younger cohort as well in those part time workers. But I think more broadly, when you look back over the last few months, we are seeing a bit of a comeback from the uncertainty around April when the when there was a bit of uncertainty around that conflict in Iran. We saw a rise in employment in May. We've seen a bigger one here in in June. But that was coming off a, you know, a bit of uncertainty in April.
episode_title: Australia's jobs surprise has one big catch

headline: ABS observes rising participation rate — particularly among women and youth — potentially driven by cost-of-living pressures rather than labour demand
reasoning: The participation rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 67% in June, the highest since May of the prior year, with youth participation up 0.6 percentage points. Crick acknowledged the narrative that this could be demand-driven in the sense that cost-of-living pressures are forcing more Australians into the labour force to supplement household incomes, particularly in part-time roles. While the ABS survey does not capture exact respondent motivations, Crick noted that increasing female and youth participation alongside part-time growth is consistent with that interpretation.
quote: We've certainly heard that narrative. And, um, yeah, well, we don't get the exact, exact reasoning from our respondents in the survey, and that certainly seems to be a trend coming through where we're seeing, you know, the part time increase. We're seeing the increasing Female participation. As you mentioned, the participation rate up 0.3 to. To 67, which is the highest since May last year. Um, again, the you know, the youth, the youth side there as well. Participation rate was up 0.6 there. So. Yeah we're seeing it I guess people entering the the labor market there. And as you say that could be quite demand driven.
episode_title: Australia's jobs surprise has one big catch

headline: ABS notes rising underemployment to 6.5% as part-time surge masks weak hours growth and workers seek more hours than available
reasoning: Crick highlighted that underemployment reached 6.5% in June, up from a recent low of 5.7% in December 2024, which he linked directly to the surge in part-time employment. Workers entering part-time roles are not necessarily getting the hours they want or need, a dynamic also reflected in hours-worked growth being considerably softer than headline employment growth. This divergence signals that while the labour market looks robust on the headline number, there is underlying slack growing in terms of hours utilisation.
quote: Underemployment. We're seeing that increase in part time, which which plays into that a little bit as well. So people they're wanting more hours and they're necessarily getting and we probably saw that a little bit in the hours work growth as well, which wasn't as strong as the employment growth this month. Um, again, being driven by the fact that we've got more people going into part time work and perhaps what not work in the hours they want.
episode_title: Australia's jobs surprise has one big catch
